Neonatal individuals of the seven-banded armadillo emerge at a modest body mass, with newborns typically weighing approximately 70 grams [Wwb = approximately 70 grams]. This relatively low birth weight is consistent with the reproductive strategy observed among Dasypus species, where females produce litters of genetically identical quadruplets following a single fertilisation event. The provision of maternal care through lactation is relatively brief; under the standard thermoneutral conditions of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C], young are fully weaned and capable of independent feeding just 60 days after birth [tx = 60 days after birth]. This rapid weaning period, lasting a mere two months, is comparatively short for a mammal of this body size and may be linked to the energetic demands placed on the mother following the birth of multiple offspring. The ability of the pups to transition to solid food at such an early stage reflects a degree of precocial development, enabling them to exploit abundant invertebrate resources in their environment shortly after the cessation of nursing.

Conception in the seven-banded armadillo is followed by an extended gestation period that lasts 132 days [tg = 132 days] when measured at the species' typical resting body temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C]. This developmental interval, spanning over four months, includes a well-documented period of embryonic diapause, wherein the blastocyst remains unimplanted for several weeks before organogenesis commences. This delay, a common feature among xenarthrans, ensures that parturition coincides with periods of peak food availability, thereby increasing neonatal survival prospects. The gestation period of this species is shorter than that of the giant armadillo, yet it is notably longer than what might be predicted for a mammal with an ultimate adult wet weight of only 1475 grams [Wwi = 1475 grams]. The relatively low adult mass, which for most wild-caught individuals rarely exceeds 1.5 kilograms, appears to be constrained by the species' predominantly myrmecophagous diet rather than by any physiological limitation on growth potential.

Puberty in the seven-banded armadillo, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the capacity to reproduce, occurs relatively late for an animal of its size. At the stable internal temperature of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C] that characterises this species' thermoregulatory set point, females reach sexual maturity at 274 days after birth [tp = 274 days after birth]. This period of approximately nine months between birth and reproductive activation is substantially longer than the interval observed in similarly sized didelphid marsupials, reflecting a slower pace of life history that is a hallmark of the family Dasypodidae. The extended juvenile phase may allow for the development of the sophisticated olfactory and foraging skills necessary to locate subsurface prey efficiently. Following the attainment of puberty, females do not immediately commence breeding at their maximum potential rate; instead, reproductive activity is modulated by environmental conditions, with many young adults deferring their first litter until their second calendar year of life.

Female seven-banded armadillos exhibit a constrained reproductive output that aligns with their relatively slow life history. Based on a typical interbirth interval and clutch size, the maximum reproductive rate is equivalent to approximately 7 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 7 offspring per year] when calculated under the species' preferred thermoneutral zone of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C]. This annual output is achieved through a combination of a single litter of four genetically identical pups per reproductive event [N_R_i = four genetically identical pups per reproductive event] and the capacity to produce just under two such litters each year [F_R_i = two such litters each year]. The obligate polyembryony that produces quadruplets is a unique adaptation among mammals and results in all littermates being the same sex, which has interesting consequences for local population genetics. The low annual fecundity, by mammalian standards, means that population growth is slow and that the species is vulnerable to overharvesting or habitat disturbance, particularly because reproductive rates cannot be elevated to compensate for increased adult mortality.

Maximum longevity in the seven-banded armadillo is considerable given its body size, with the oldest documented individuals living approximately 16.8 years [am = approximately 16.8 years] under the stable thermal conditions of 34.5 °C [T = 34.5 °C]. This remarkable lifespan, exceeding sixteen years, places D. septemcinctus among the longest-lived xenarthrans relative to body size and is thought to be linked to the species' low basal metabolic rate and its occupation of a relatively predation-free niche, as the thick, articulated carapace provides effective defence against most natural predators. The ultimate wet weight of 1475 grams [Wwi = 1475 grams] represents a plateau that most individuals approach by their third year, after which somatic growth effectively ceases and maintenance metabolism dominates energy expenditure. This combination of a small adult body size, a protracted juvenile period, and exceptional longevity positions the seven-banded armadillo as an extreme example of a slow life history strategy within the mammalian order Cingulata.
